text: At the Vetra QBR, their director opened by saying he was evaluating competitors. Instead of defending Lumina right away, I spent twenty minutes just mapping what had changed in their operation and brought three of those points to the roadmap meeting the following week. The renewal closed with a plan upgrade.

I spent Thursday afternoon migrating our accounts from the old master spreadsheet into the new CRM and scheduling the tool trainings for the team. Nothing glamorous, but everything was ready before the end of the day.

Our weekly portfolio meeting kept turning into venting with no conclusions. Juliana set up a fixed three-block agenda, makes it clear who decides what, and closes every topic with an owner and a deadline. These days we leave the room in forty minutes with everything on track.

When Juliana missed the deadline to send the Grupo Almeida renewal proposal, she brought it up herself in the team meeting before anyone asked, explained what she was going to change in her process, and asked us to flag it if we ever saw it happening again.

At the prioritization committee with product, Juliana showed up with recordings of three customers complaining about the export flow and made everyone watch them before opening the backlog. The discussion shifted from opinion to evidence, and the item moved up in priority right there.

In my first month, I gave TechNorte the wrong contract information and was terrified. Juliana pulled me aside, told me about a similar mistake she had made herself when she was a CSM, and put together the correction email to the client with me. I left that conversation wanting to get it right, not wanting to hide.

The account handoff between support and CS was a gray area and tickets kept falling into the void. Juliana got both sides into one room, drew the flow on the whiteboard, and only wrapped up once every step had a defined owner. It has been two months without a single ticket getting lost in the transition.

LogiMax's CFO joined the renewal call already announcing he was going to cancel over the price increase. I let him talk for ten minutes without interrupting, acknowledged point by point what made sense, and proposed revisiting the scope before talking price. We came out with the renewal signed for another twelve months.

After hearing the same complaint about the churn report in two consecutive QBRs, I wrote a summary with the customers' verbatim quotes and took it to the roadmap meeting with product. Two weeks later the fix made it into the quarter's plan.

Last sprint, support and engineering were trading jabs in the channel over who owned the Farmus bug. Otávio pulled the two of them into a quick chat, translated what each side was actually asking for, and the argument died right there, with the fix agreed for Thursday.

When the director at Banco Sollo sent that all-caps email threatening to escalate to the CEO, Otávio asked to join the account with me and replied in a tone that disarmed the client with the very first message. Afterwards he even stayed late reviewing the account's open tickets with me.

I shared a booth with Otávio at the customer event in São Paulo. We took turns during the peak hours, cataloged the lead badges at the end of each day, and still had time to catch two talks from the product track.

During the handover of the Orbita Foods account from sales to CS, the client was upset about promises he felt had not been kept. Otávio ran the transition meeting without pointing fingers at anyone, realigned expectations item by item, and the client ended the call saying thank you.

During the billing bug crisis, Otávio personally called each of the eight affected customers before any of them opened a ticket. The next day he even showed up at the support daily asking where he could help clear the queue. Two of the accounts praised Lumina by email after that.

While preparing the ClaraMed QBR, I interviewed four end users on top of the sponsor and discovered the field team didn't even know offline mode existed. I rebuilt the entire presentation around their day-to-day, and the sponsor asked us to repeat the format next quarter.

When I joined, I was terrified of asking a dumb question in the team channel. Aline made a habit of answering any question of mine by starting with an example of where she herself had once stumbled on the topic. These days I ask anything without thinking twice.

During the cancellation flow redesign, Aline came in with screenshots of real customer conversations showing exactly where they got stuck, and made us redo two steps that looked great internally. Offboarding NPS went up the following month.
Aline and I were put in charge of the year-end on-call schedule. We settled the date swaps in one afternoon and sent the calendar out to the team that same week.

I invited Aline to co-facilitate a round of interviews with churned customers. She opened each conversation by acknowledging what Lumina had gotten wrong with that account, and the customers relaxed and shared things that would never show up in a survey.

At the quarterly retro, Aline kicked off the conversation about the Farmus churn by first saying what she herself would have done differently, and the whole team dissected the case without anyone getting defensive. Three concrete changes to the onboarding playbook came out of it.

The TechNorte ticket looked like just an import error, but I kept pulling the thread and found that the integration job had been failing silently since the last update. I wrote up the step-by-step reproduction, opened the incident with engineering, and only marked it resolved after validating the data with the customer.
I used the quietest Friday of the month to clean up the old Zendesk macros and update the internal contact list we use to route tickets. Nothing urgent, but it had been sitting in my queue for weeks.

During the payments integration outage, the queue jumped to ninety tickets in an hour and everyone started replying in a scramble. Vítor opened a call, split the queue into three blocks, and dictated the standard response in the same voice you'd use to read a menu. Nobody panicked after that.

My first overnight on-call shift landed right on the migration window that went wrong. I called Vítor at three in the morning thinking it was the end of the world, and he walked me through it step by step, without a hint of irritation in his voice, until the service came back up.

Banco Sollo had been complaining for months about the dashboard being slow, and the standard answer was that we were monitoring it. Vítor built a load-time comparison on his own initiative, took it to engineering, and followed the case through to the deploy of the fix, updating the client at every step.

During the database incident, Vítor was our bridge to the customers. While we debugged, he sent updates every twenty minutes in a tone that kept even the most nervous accounts steady, and filtered out the noise so our side could stay focused.

When Farmus threatened to cancel over the repeated tickets, Vítor asked to be the single point of contact for the account, mapped the five recurring problems, and closed them out one by one in three weeks, even the ones that depended on other teams. The account renewed without a discount.

I joined knowing nothing about APIs and Orbita Foods kept asking about the integration. I spent two evenings on the internal webhooks course, set up a test environment to practice, and the following week I led the technical call on my own, with on-call just listening in as a safety net.

The week I had three QBRs piled up, Natália noticed without me saying a word and showed up with the usage-data decks for all three accounts already filled in. All I had to do was review them and record my commentary on top.

When we migrated the help center to a new tool, Natália was the first to master the new editor. Within two weeks she had already rewritten twenty articles and recorded a short video teaching the rest of the team, without anyone asking.

Natália took on collecting the topics for our monthly customer coffee chat and put together the agenda for the next session. It was settled that it will stay in the online format, on the last Thursday of the month.

I was stuck with a list of prospects who had previously been Lumina customers and couldn't figure out their cancellation reasons. Natália, who isn't even on my team, offered to go through them account by account with me during a free hour of her on-call shift and walked me through the history of each one.

I gave Natália the most technical account in the portfolio almost as a test. Within a month she absorbed the vocabulary of the logistics sector, rebuilt LogiMax's success plan with metrics that made sense to the client, and switched approaches quickly when the first proposal didn't land.

I noticed that Vetra's tickets kept coming in with the same manual export request. I called to understand their routine, documented the use case, and brought to the product meeting the numbers on how much time the customer was losing per week because of it.
This week I updated my email signature to the company's new standard and archived the old folders of closed tickets. While I was at it, I deleted some reply drafts I never got around to using.

We split the legacy ticket migration push and Eduardo nailed it: he promised his four hundred by Friday and delivered Thursday night, with the log of every batch recorded in the spreadsheet. It's the kind of commitment we don't even need to double-check with him.

Whenever I promise a customer of mine an update on an escalated ticket, Eduardo is the one on the other end. In the last three ClaraMed cases, he got back to me on the exact date he had agreed with me, including one where he had to chase two other teams to keep the deadline from slipping.

In triage, Eduardo doesn't close a ticket by fixing just the symptom. In the Grupo Almeida case, he picked up from the tone of the messages that the real problem was the client's accounting close, raised the priority, and explained that context to engineering right in the ticket.

I needed usage data for ten accounts for the renewals task force, and Eduardo was the only one who delivered the complete package on the agreed date, even with the support queue slammed that week. I didn't even have to send a reminder.

On the project to reduce first-response time, Eduardo took on the four-hour target and closed three straight weeks within the goal, adjusting his own shift to cover the hours when retail customers open the most tickets.

At the quarterly retro I told everyone that the decision to postpone the Postgres migration had been mine and that it cost us two weeks of rework. I'd rather own the mistake in front of everyone than let the team think the problem was their planning. After that, our conversations about estimates became much more candid.

I spent a good part of Tuesday reviewing next semester's cloud budget with the finance team. I also took the chance to update the cost-per-service spreadsheet and schedule the renewal of our observability tool licenses.

The release 4.2 planning was turning into a shouting match over estimates when Sofia stopped everything, listed the three decisions that had to come out of that meeting and gave each person two minutes to speak. We left in forty minutes with scope closed and owners assigned for every epic. It's impressive how meetings with her in charge end with decisions made.

I agreed with Sofia that the billing service tech debt would go into the next sprint and, I admit, I let it slip. On Monday she showed up at my desk with the agreement written down and asked me what I needed to hit the deadline. With her, nothing we agree on in a meeting ever falls through the cracks.

In the post-mortem for the gateway outage, Sofia opened by saying she herself had approved the deploy without a contingency window, before anyone could point fingers. That changed the tone of the room instantly: everyone started describing what they did without fear. The final document came out with five action items and no scapegoats.

When the commitment to cover the regression tests before the freeze started slipping, Sofia pulled me and Tomás in and rebuilt the plan with dates and owners in front of everyone. The following week she came back to the topic in the daily herself to check on progress, item by item.

In my first sprint I was lost between three demands, and Sofia set up a quick session with Caio and Marina to align priorities and split up who would support me on what. In half an hour everyone left knowing exactly their part. She has a way of organizing people that just makes the work move.

Bruno and Tomás had been stuck for two days arguing whether the notifications service should use a queue or webhooks, and the mood in the channel had already soured. I pulled the two of them into a room, asked each one to write the trade-offs on the whiteboard and proposed a one-day load test to decide with numbers. They left to have lunch together and the decision came the next day.

In the discussion about carving up the monolith, André and I were already trading jabs in a thread when Marina stepped in, summarized both sides with impressive neutrality and suggested taking the matter to the RFC instead of the chat. The tension died right there and the RFC got approved with no hard feelings.

I handed Marina the log audit epic with a tight deadline because of the certification. She broke it into weekly deliverables, flagged on Wednesday that one item would slip two days and made it up on the next one. She closed the epic on the agreed date, with no surprises at all.

There was a week when product and engineering got stuck over the export report deadline, with people complaining on both sides. Marina offered to sit down with me and João and translated the fight into two scope options with realistic dates. A meeting that promised to be tense ended in agreement in twenty minutes.

I shared the new office workbench with Marina during the third-floor renovation. We ended up syncing our focus hours and the rotation for the small meeting room. Other than that, it was an ordinary sprint week.

When Letícia got buried in design system bugs right before the freeze, Marina noticed before I did and took on two fixes without anyone asking. She has also been my thermometer for the team: when a technical discussion starts heating up, she steps in and brings everyone back to the problem. She is the person who keeps the temperature of the room in check.

Before we approved switching the event bus, I built a matrix comparing cost, latency and maturity across the three options and ran a weekend prototype with real data. The result knocked out the option that was my favorite, and it was the first one I discarded. I'd rather lose a personal bet than push a decision without evidence.

This sprint I was on interview duty for the technical loops and reviewed the system design question script with the recruiting folks. I also migrated my architecture notes to the new wiki. Busy week, but nothing out of the ordinary.

My first code review at Lumina came back with seventeen comments from Caio and none of them was just 'change this': each one explained the why and linked an example in our codebase. Afterwards he set aside half an hour to pair with me on the concurrency part I hadn't understood. In two months I grew more than in the entire previous year.

In the design of the new permissions API, Caio was the only one who asked what would happen when the cache expired mid-session, and he dismantled the proposal with two scenarios nobody had considered. We redid the design and avoided what would have been a guaranteed incident in production.

When I took over the event pipeline, Caio put together a three-week study plan with me and reviewed my diagrams every Friday, always pointing out where my reasoning skipped a step. He doesn't give you the answer: he asks the question that forces you to find it yourself.

As a PM, I've seen tech leads let roadmap agreements evaporate, but with Caio it's the opposite: he records every commitment from the sprint review and follows up, including with me, when something drifts. Last quarter he called me in to publicly renegotiate an item engineering wasn't going to deliver, instead of letting it die quietly.

Caio instituted a biweekly review of technical debt items on the team and won't let an item leave the list without an owner and a date. When the messaging queue discussion heated up, he brought benchmarks and a failure comparison before giving an opinion. He is my most reliable counterpoint on hard decisions.

When the Vetra data migration corrupted a customer dashboard on a Friday, I called engineering expecting a ticket number and got Caio in our war room fifteen minutes later. He explained the failure to my team without a single acronym, set a fix deadline for Monday and met it. He treats a customer incident as his problem, not as an interruption.

I asked Caio for help on a technical call with the Sollux architects expecting a generic slide deck; he showed up having read the prospect's integration docs and sketched the data flow live with them. Half of the objections died right there. He still follows up with me after every deal to hear what the customer actually asked.

The usage report that feeds billing drifted from the product numbers and Caio spent an afternoon with me tracing the divergence to a duplicated event in the pipeline. He wrote the reconciliation runbook himself and now pings me on the first of every month to check that the totals still match.

During the March outage I was the one answering angry chats, and Caio kept a live thread translating what the platform team was doing into words I could pass to customers, every ten minutes, until service came back. Nobody asked him to do it. It was the calmest I have ever seen support feel in the middle of an incident.

I picked up the billing service rewrite in January with a commitment to flip the switch before the fiscal close. I sliced the migration into seven deliverables, posted progress every Friday in the channel and we cut over with three days to spare. There was no heroism, just the plan being executed week after week.

Reviewing one of Bruno's PRs, I noticed he had left comments in his own code flagging two timezone edge cases that not even my tests covered. He also attached to the description a table with the cent-rounding scenarios he had validated manually. It's rare for QA to find anything after he reviews his own work.

I split the new payment provider integration with Bruno and we agreed he would deliver the reconciliation layer by the 20th. On the 18th it was in production behind a feature flag, with a runbook written. Working with him means being able to plan on his word.

Every month-end I depend on the reconciliation job Bruno maintains to close the operations numbers. On one of those closes he alerted me to a four-cent discrepancy the old system had been ignoring for months, along with the query proving its origin. We closed the month without a manual adjustment for the first time this year.

For the office move, Bruno took charge of labeling the workbench equipment and organizing the spare cables in the cabinet. We also took the opportunity to update the monitor inventory with the facilities folks.

Over the last six sprints Bruno delivered everything he pulled, and when he realized the idempotency story was bigger than it looked, he flagged it in Monday's daily and replanned with me, not at the last minute. It's the kind of predictability that lets me sleep soundly during release week.

Before releasing the new invoices screen, I put together a checklist of the empty, error and loading states across three screen sizes, and found a layout overflow that only showed up with very long company names. I fixed it and added the case to the visual test suite so it wouldn't come back.

I was drowning trying to finish the onboarding form and hadn't even asked for help when Letícia showed up with a draft branch solving the validation part that was blocking me. She had noticed from the channel that I was going in circles. She then stayed with me until the end of the day reviewing the rest.

In the export flow review, Letícia listed eight inconsistencies in date and currency masks across screens that had been slipping through for months. Everything came documented with screenshots and step-by-step reproduction. My QA work yields twice as much when the PR is hers.

I delivered the redesign of the table components and Letícia returned an implementation with spacing and focus states faithful to the spec down to the pixel, including a keyboard state I myself had forgotten to design. She even pointed out two inconsistencies in my Figma file.
I heard Letícia took over organizing the team's World Cup pool and the schedule for the Friday demo rotation. In this week's dailies we only synced on merging the release branch, a quiet week.

Twice this quarter Letícia reshuffled her own tasks to rescue swamped teammates, once on the checkout accessibility fixes and once on the freeze bug queue, without me having to ask. And she remains the person who catches the most visual problems before QA even takes a look.

When the production cluster started killing pods at 3 a.m., I opened the incident call, assigned who would look at the database and who would look at the network, and narrated every hypothesis we tested in the channel. In forty minutes we isolated the memory leak, and only then did I go figure out why the alert was late. Panic doesn't diagnose anything.
I finished documenting the access key rotation process and updated the network topology diagram on the wiki. I also left the quarterly maintenance of the CI runners scheduled for the holiday.

On the Friday of the DNS provider blackout, with half the platform down and sales panicking in the general channel, André kept replying in the same tone as always, listing what we already knew and what still needed confirming. He asked for ten minutes of operational silence, applied the failover and we were back before the SLA blew.

The flaky test that kept breaking our deploy wasn't even André's domain, but it bothered him, so he traced the cause down to a race condition in the sessions service and opened the fix along with a new alert. He carried the problem all the way to the end when he could have just forwarded the ticket.

I work on the support front line and have been in several war rooms with André. In the December queue overflow, he gave me updates every fifteen minutes with what I could relay internally, without a note of stress in his voice. The recovery estimate he gave was off by only ten minutes.

André promised the observability migration wouldn't cause a single minute of downtime and delivered exactly that, with a rollback plan rehearsed in staging twice. The new dashboards became a reference for the whole team.

In the replica database incident, André took command without me having to assign anyone, coordinated three people with a calm that soothed even folks outside engineering, and then wrote the most thorough post-mortem I have ever received. He treats any platform problem as his own until someone formally takes it over.

We needed to swap the pipeline orchestrator and I had never touched Airflow. I spent a weekend with the documentation and a toy cluster, and on Wednesday I presented a comparison based on what I had actually tested, including the points where my initial hypothesis was wrong. I changed my recommendation halfway through the study because the numbers didn't support the first one.

On the proposal to double the data cluster, Paula asked for a week, came back with a cost-per-query analysis and showed the bottleneck was a badly partitioned join, not capacity. We saved the entire expansion because she wouldn't accept the obvious diagnosis.

Paula and I shared the presentation slot at last month's all-hands to show the internal roadmap for the data platform. We rehearsed the day before in the big room and everything went fine with the new projector.

I asked Paula for help with a data cross-reference for my latest study and discovered she had taught herself, in two weeks, the statistical analysis library my team took months to adopt. She even sent me back a reproducible notebook commenting on every decision in the model.

When we migrated the events to the new schema, Paula was the only one who had never worked with Protobuf, and within ten days she was already reviewing my PRs, pointing out compatibility gotchas I didn't know about. She turns documentation into practice at an impressive speed.

Before any expensive decision on the data platform I run it by Paula: she breaks the proposal down into assumptions, tests the ones that can be tested and hands me back the risk in numbers. That's how we avoided signing an oversized warehouse contract last quarter.

I joined Lumina having never touched Go, and three months later I was running the reprocessing worker on my own. I kept an error journal of my first weeks and went back to it every Friday so I wouldn't repeat the same stumbles. What helped me most was asking for review early, before the code was pretty.

The task force to cut build time had been dragging on for two sprints until Diego rallied a one-afternoon blitz, with a scoreboard of minutes saved on the whiteboard. His energy won over even the people who had said they had no time, and the build dropped from 22 to 9 minutes that week.

I borrowed Diego to help me on the front end for a sprint and he had never touched React. By the third day he was already opening decent PRs, and by the end of the sprint he fixed a state bug on his own that would have taken me an afternoon. He writes everything down and never asks the same question twice.

I needed an API prototype to validate the reports flow before the roadmap review and Diego volunteered on the spot, put the skeleton together the same day and kept sending me updates in the evening without me asking. His pace unblocked a discussion that had been stalled for two weeks.
Diego took charge of updating the on-call rotation in the shared calendar after the team's timezone change. Together we double-checked the semester's holidays and adjusted the agreed swaps.

Diego is the junior who got off training wheels fastest on the team: in four months he went from guided tasks to driving the modernization of the queue jobs on his own. In plannings he is always the first to volunteer, and more than once his enthusiasm pulled the sprint out of inertia after a rough week.

During the 4.1 release regression, I got suspicious about a one-pixel difference in the totals column and pulled the thread: it was a rounding issue that added up wrong only on invoices with installment discounts. I wrote the test case, mapped the three affected screens and held the release until the fix landed.
I spent the morning reorganizing the test evidence repository by release and archiving the old plans. In the afternoon I attended the semester's mandatory information security training.

I thought my billing module PR was bulletproof until Renata sent back a script with fourteen scenarios, including a leap-year month rollover that broke the pro rata calculation. She even had test data ready to reproduce it. Nothing gets past her.

At the start of the freeze we agreed no critical bug would go to production without a full regression, and when I tried to open an exception 'just this once', Renata reminded me of the agreement in front of the team and proposed a path that fit the deadline. She holds everyone to what was agreed, senior folks included.

I forwarded engineering some odd behavior in the consumption report and Renata was the one who took the case. She reproduced the scenario with three configuration combinations I didn't even know existed and sent me back a step-by-step of what was wrong in each one. The ticket came back more complete than I sent it.

Renata owns our definition of done: when the team started loosening the minimum coverage on end-of-quarter deliveries, she brought the numbers to the retro and got us to renew the agreement in writing. Since then she is the one who audits, release by release, whether we are keeping what we signed.

I took on delivering the export module with a date promised for the quarter close, and I cut two improvements I had proposed myself when I saw they put the date at risk. We delivered on the agreed day and the improvements went into the following sprint. I'd rather ship the essentials on time than everything late.

I upgraded my machine to the new container-based development setup and took the chance to re-record the technical onboarding video that had been outdated since last year. I also replaced the keyboard that was failing.

Every quarter we bet on who delivers what they planned, and with Tomás it's not even fun: over the last four releases he nailed the scope without slipping a single day. When the PDF service threatened to run late, he renegotiated the cut on Monday, not the day before the demo.

In the dispute over which squad would own the reports service, Tomás gave up a project that would clearly have earned him the spotlight because the other path unblocked the release for the whole team. He presented the transition plan himself. Ego doesn't enter the equation for him when the team's goal is at stake.

Whenever Tomás hands me a deploy window, I block my calendar without a second thought: the artifact arrives tested, with the rollback checklist filled out and at the time he said. In two years of on-call together, I have never had to chase him.

The revenue recognition report depended on an extraction engineering never prioritized, until Tomás took it on. He delivered the first version to me on the Friday he promised and automated the monthly send without me asking. I close the financials two days earlier because of it.

When I had to choose who would carry the certification release delivery, I chose Tomás and he reprioritized the squad's backlog around the date, pulling even his own items out of the way. He is the person I use as my benchmark for predictability when I negotiate deadlines with other areas.

During the quarter close, I kept a spreadsheet open with every pending item and the name of whoever had taken it on. The following Monday, I went through them one by one chasing what hadn't been delivered, including my own. Nobody is entirely comfortable with it, but nothing falls through the cracks.

We received three payroll system proposals and the two cheapest looked great on paper. I spent a weekend building a three-year total cost comparison before deciding. I ended up choosing the most expensive one on paper, which was the cheapest in the real-world scenario.

During the external audit, Patrícia owned up in front of the auditor to a classification error that had come from a decision of hers and brought the correction plan the next day. Then she followed up with each of us on the plan's items, with a deadline and an owner defined.

When I proposed a new benefits program, Patrícia cut precisely the part that was most my style and kept what reached the entire team. It stung in the moment, but she was right: the budget went to what moved the needle, not to anyone's pet project.

I brought Patrícia a proposal to automate the reconciliation and she took my estimate apart in ten minutes, with the numbers from the last close in hand. I redid the case with better assumptions and she approved it on the spot. I'd take that scrutiny over an empty yes any day.

At the end of the year, Patrícia gave up two hires in her own area to protect the cash that secured the collective bonus. And she explained why to us with no beating around the bush, in a fifteen-minute meeting.

During offsite week, Patrícia shared the airport van with me and we spent the ride talking about the renovation of the big meeting room. Once we arrived, we each went off to handle our own part of the agenda.

Before sending payroll to the bank, I always run a line-by-line check against the previous month. This month I caught a duplicated night-shift premium that would have slipped through and turned into rework for everyone later.

In the June close, Henrique found a twelve-cent difference in the reconciliation and wouldn't rest until he traced its origin, an entry booked to the wrong account. And he still reminded me of our agreement to document the adjustment before rolling over the month.

I asked Henrique to review the financial annexes of a large contract and he came back with three inconsistencies between the draft and the pricing spreadsheet that not even the other party's legal team had spotted. We signed with the correct figures because of that review.
Henrique and I were in charge of picking the restaurant for the department's year-end dinner. We traded about ten links in the chat and ended up booking the same place as last year.

Every month I send the commissions base to Henrique and, if I'm a day late, he's already at my desk chasing it, rightly so. Since he took over that workflow, not a single commission has gone out wrong or late.

In the audit preparation, Henrique reviewed folder by folder and found two receipts with the wrong date before the auditor asked for anything. Then he chased every department until the last document arrived on time, without me having to step in.

During new-hire onboarding, I always tell the story of the mistake I made on my first payroll run here. I notice that, after that, people start bringing me questions they would be embarrassed to take to their manager.
I spent Tuesday updating the org chart in the HR system because two people changed teams. While I was at it, I fixed some job titles that had been out of date since last year.

A manager and one of his reports had spent weeks trading passive-aggressive remarks over denied vacation days, and Carolina sat down with both of them in the same room. They left with a schedule agreement and the matter died right there. She has a way of lowering the temperature without letting anyone off the hook.

During payroll close week I was drowning and hadn't even asked for help. Carolina noticed, took over the triage of the benefits tickets, and even left a chocolate on my desk. I only realized how big the help was once the peak had passed.

Two of my engineers were locked in an argument about working from home that was already contaminating the rest of the team, and I called Carolina. She led the difficult conversation I had been putting off and the two of them walked out with a written agreement. She's the person I go to when the topic is thorny.

When the health plan change was announced, the mood soured at the all-hands and Carolina took over the room. She gave the floor first to the people who were angriest, without cutting anyone off, and turned an explosive agenda item into a civilized conversation.

During the review cycle, two managers from other areas nearly fell out in a calibration session and Carolina mediated the session until they left with a shared criterion. Beyond that, she was the one who had the new analyst's back through her first payroll run, without anyone asking.

The travel expense report wasn't even mine, but it kept running late and blocking everyone's close. I took over the process, automated the receipt collection, and today it goes out two days ahead of the deadline.

Every month on the 25th, Lucas hands me the bank reconciliations closed, and in two years I can't remember a single delay. For the accounting close I build my schedule on top of his delivery with my eyes closed.
Lucas and I split the task of receiving the air-conditioning maintenance technicians on Friday. He took the morning, I took the afternoon, and we used the time to update the room inventory.

We discovered a transit-benefit deduction error affecting about thirty people, and the matter wasn't even in Lucas's scope. He mapped the cases, calculated the reimbursements, and only let go of the issue once the last colleague confirmed the correction on the following payroll.

I ask Lucas for the cost-per-squad numbers at the start of every quarter and the answer always arrives ahead of the agreed date, in the format we aligned on a single time. It has become the part of my planning I simply don't worry about.

When the bank changed the payment file layout in the middle of the close, Lucas rewrote the routine overnight and payroll landed in everyone's account on the right day. He didn't bring me the problem, he brought me the problem already solved.

Before approving the new standard client contract, I listed the five risks that had already turned into disputes in old contracts and tested the new draft against each one. Two clauses fell in that fine-tooth-comb review and went back for redrafting.
I spent the morning reorganizing the contract repository by year and by counterparty, which had been a mess since the system migration. Now at least search actually finds things.

We were about to deadlock with a vendor over a penalty clause, and Tânia drafted an alternative that protected Lumina without humiliating the other side. She closed in one week what had been stuck for a month. On top of that, she found a company-registration number discrepancy in the annexes that nobody had spotted.

My team came in fuming because legal had blocked an aggressive discount, and Tânia, instead of hammering on the rule, built with us an annual contract format that passed compliance and that the client accepted on the spot. We all left the room feeling like we had won.
